entries.subject: A military engineer's bastioned-fortification drawing with plain brass dividers.
entries.brief: ONE almost-white folded MILITARY ENGINEER'S PLAN on a compact broad rectangular sheet, shown in an elevated modest three-quarter view, just one small upper corner curled. A clear large geometric outline of a BASTIONED FORT occupies most of the sheet: central pentagonal enceinte, FIVE outward-projecting angular bastions connected logically by curtain walls, a narrow surrounding ditch line and restrained faint red/ochre earthwork fills. This is a technical plan in dark charcoal and muted brick-red ink, NOT a real miniature castle or city. Each bastion is a broad pentagonal salient with two faces and two flanks, not merely a star-shaped symbol; no medieval towers, city buildings or scenery. ONE simple aged brass DIVIDER with two slender metal pointed legs rests diagonally across one lower corner, clear of the central outline. Both legs join correctly at a single hinge; no disconnected tips or added third leg. Paper close to white, clear plan linework, gentle paper folds. No decorative writing, scale numbers, names, arrows, title panel or surrounding parchment frame.

refs.title: Bastioned fortification — Musée des Plans-Reliefs
refs.note: Museum teaching diagram explains bastions, curtain walls and ditch. Our simplified pentagonal plan is conceptual, not a copy of a particular fortified city.

refs.title: Historical fortification drawing of Gravelines — Italian Ministry of Culture
refs.note: Image search supplied a period ink plan as material/composition context; direct page open failed. No image was copied.

entries.subject: Historical brass gunner's callipers measuring one iron round shot.
entries.brief: ONE HISTORICAL GUNNER'S CALLIPER actively MEASURING A SINGLE IRON CANNONBALL. The dominant instrument has two substantial aged BRASS arms joined by one secure hinged pivot, with two short curved dark IRON measuring tips. It is opened around the round shot: the tips touch two diametrically opposed sides of the same sphere, a physically coherent external-diameter measurement. The single dense charcoal-grey forged iron cannonball sits between the jaws, visibly smaller than the complete opened calliper silhouette. The top brass arms carry a few simple unlabeled measurement ticks, NO modern sliding vernier, micrometer, digital readout, numbers or readable inscriptions. Ball and tool form a single connected functional concept, not a stockpile or finished-goods display. Complete calliper and full cannonball visible, generous margins. Subdued warm brass and neutral dark iron with restrained matte patina; readable metallic edges, no shiny fantasy gold. No fuse, exploding shell, flame, hammer, cannon carriage, three-ball pyramid, table, arms, human or other accessory.

refs.title: Gunner's callipers, brass with iron tips — Science Museum Group
refs.note: Museum instrument by Dominicus Lusuerg, maker active 1694–1744; measures cannon bore or round-shot diameter. Simplified external-measurement concept, not exact inscribed facsimile.

refs.title: Gribeauval system — Musée de l'Armée
refs.note: Primary museum explains dimensional plans, manufacture quality and standardized components. Illustration shows inspection of caliber, not every part of the system.

entries.subject: A wooden plane table with brass sighting alidade on an oak tripod.
entries.brief: ONE HISTORICAL SURVEYING PLANE TABLE with a SIMPLE SIGHTING ALIDADE, all shown in a compact elevated three-quarter view. A modest square warm-brown wooden drawing board is securely attached at its center to a visible small brass ball-and-socket mounting joint over an oak THREE-LEGGED TRIPOD. Exactly three structurally attached tripod legs, naturally splayed, complete feet inside canvas; no extra sticks or detached foot. A near-white drawing sheet is clipped flat directly to the table surface; its faint charcoal linework suggests a few hill contours and sighting rays, no cadastral parcel grid and no readable text. ONE brass alidade straightedge lies flat ON the sheet, with exactly TWO slender upright sighting vanes properly attached at its two endpoints. Each vane has a small open sighting slot, no giant telescope or microscope. The straightedge visibly connects both vanes, no unsupported floating parts. All components form ONE working instrument. Warm wood, subdued brass, nearly-white paper; no blue cast. No loose rolled map, measuring chain, compass, sextant, terrain patch, mountain scenery, standing surveyor, room or backdrop.

refs.title: Plane table outfit including alidade — Science Museum Group
refs.note: W. & S. Jones outfit, 1801–1830, board, alidade and tripod. Museum sheet is modern replacement; icon linework is a conceptual map, not copied historical paper.

refs.title: Plane-table survey principles — Historic England
refs.note: Modern official technical description confirms functional connections and sighting vanes; not used to date the historical tool.
